title: Sunfall observing campaign
question: What can you honestly say about the Sun, the Moon, and an orbit from what you measure here?

intro.speaker: Ranger Wren
lines: Ridgeline to Sunfall. The notebooks from last year do not agree. One says the noon Sun sits higher in January.
Rebuild the record from this ground. The sky is the lab. You stay on it.

completeJournalEntry.title: Observation window
completeJournalEntry.text: The campaign has a window: night on the mesa rim, a thin Moon, and the return predicted from the orbit. The sky did what the notes said it would.

gnomon.name: Solar marker
gnomon.prompt: Record the shadow. Direction, length, time. Then do it again when the light has changed.

moonSite.name: Night-sky viewpoint
moonSite.prompt: From the mesa the station lights fall away. Log the Moon from here.

compareSample.name: Drawer sample
compareSample.text: A labeled fragment in the observatory drawer: dark, dense, a fused rind. If you found a rock like this on the crater floor, you would have something to compare.

idle: Start at the solar marker. Morning, noon, afternoon. Do not tell me what you think the Sun does until the shadows argue.
afterShadows: Three times, one post. The shadow moved. Apparent motion is not yet an explanation.
afterRotation: Same post, other dates. Winter, an equinox, summer — noon each time. Watch height, day length, and how far Earth sits from the Sun.
afterSeasons: Sandskip-1 is a tracked rock. We have its distance from the Sun and not its period. The orbit table will take a number.
afterOrbit: The Moon does not need a poster of eight pictures. Log it from the mesa. Then move the model.
afterMoon: If the Moon goes around every month, why is there not an eclipse every month? The alignment model is on the dome table.
afterEclipse: A coastal station sent tide range. We are not studying oceans here. We are asking whether the Moon and Sun leave a fingerprint in that table.
afterData: The campaign needs a window. Where you stand, when you look, what the Moon is doing, and when Sandskip returns. Write a plan you can defend.
afterSuccess: Sunfall will still be here at night. High Country and Cedar Hollow too. The tools stay with the tablet.

rotationChoices.label: The Sun races around Earth each day.
Earth turns. The Sun only appears to move.

seasonChoices.label: Summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun.
Earth's tilt changes Sun angle and day length.

eclipseChoices.label: There is an eclipse every month; we just miss them.
The Moon's path is tilted, so alignments usually miss.

tideChoices.label: Largest ranges sit with new and full Moon.
The range is just weather at the coast.
The range does not change with the Moon.

planetChoices.label: Farther objects take longer to go around. Dense worlds cluster inward.
The names in order are the science.

challenge.title: The Observation Window
challenge.goal: Sandskip-1 will be faint. Choose a site, a time, a Moon, and the return you predicted.

reasons.label: Open horizon — the rim does not eat the target
Dark sky — sunlight and station glow stay out of the way
The orbit says the object is back
